title: Mount Sterling / Little Mountain Town
summary: Mount Sterling grew beside an Adena burial mound called the Little Mountain, where Hugh Forbes sold lots around 1790 before the town’s 1792 charter.
bodyMarkdown:
Mount Sterling takes its name from two places: an ancient Native earthwork the first settlers called "the Little Mountain," and the Scottish town of Stirling. [A history of Mount Sterling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Sterling,_Kentucky) explains that developer Hugh Forbes named the town, and that the 1792 act establishing it spelled the name "Mt. Sterling." The misspelling stuck.

## The Little Mountain

Long before Kentucky's pioneer era, Adena people built a large burial mound here roughly 2,000 years ago. Explorers, hunters and surveyors traveling a path known as Old Harper's Trace noted the tree-covered mound. Later excavation confirmed that it was a burial site. The mound stood at what is now the corner of Queen and Locust streets in downtown Mount Sterling.

The sources disagree on its size. The mound stood about 25 feet high and 125 feet across until the city removed it in 1845, according to [Kentucky Historical Society marker 2290](https://history.ky.gov/markers/little-mountain-indian-mound). The [Grokipedia entry on Mount Sterling](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mount_Sterling,_Kentucky) mentions finds such as shell necklaces and copper beads. The [Grokipedia entry on the Adena culture](https://grokipedia.com/page/Adena_culture) describes the wider tradition of mound building across the Ohio Valley. Similar mounds are told in [Ashland's Adena mounds](/stories/ashlands-adena-mounds/).

## Settlers and surveyors

The first cabin in the area was built in 1779. The land drew some of Kentucky's earliest land speculators. [William Calk](/stories/william-calks-1775-journal/), whose 1775 journal records the trip into Kentucky, later settled on Hinkston Creek near the future town.

Forbes, a Scotsman, and surveyor Enoch Smith were the main founders. Around 1790 they began selling lots. In 1792 the town was established on 640 acres owned by Smith, Forbes, John Judy and Samuel Spurgin. Nearby stations, such as Smith's Station to the north, gave settlers some shared protection during years of conflict with Native nations who still contested the region.

## A county seat

When Montgomery County was formed from Clark County, Mount Sterling became its seat. The [Grokipedia entry on Montgomery County](https://grokipedia.com/page/Montgomery_County,_Kentucky) dates the county's creation to December 14, 1796, with the boundaries taking effect in March 1797. The town entry says Mount Sterling was named seat in 1796, while the county entry says 1797. The county was named for Gen. Richard Montgomery, killed at Quebec in 1775.

The town was laid out with 33 lots at that time. A brick market house where farm produce was bought and sold soon confirmed the town as the area's commercial center. It was formally incorporated as a city in 1852.

## Kentucky today

Mount Sterling remains the Montgomery County seat. Its October Court Day festival grew out of the county court sessions that once drew settlers to town for trading and business, and Grokipedia calls it Kentucky's oldest continuously running public event. The mound that gave the town its first name no longer stands at Queen and Locust.
